OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $G$ be a graph with $n$ vertices and $\delta n^{2}$ edges. Are there subgraphs $H_1,H_2\subseteq G$ such that
$H_1$ has $\gg \delta^3n^2$ edges and every two edges in $H_1$ are contained in a cycle of length at most $6$, and furthermore if two edges share a vertex they are on a cycle of length $4$, and
$H_2$ has $\gg \delta^2n^2$ edges and every two edges in $H_2$ are contained in a cycle of length at most $8$.
#584: [DuEr82][DER84]
graph theory | 
cycles
A problem of Erdős, Duke, and Rödl. Duke and Erdős [DuEr82] proved the first if $n$ is sufficiently large depending on $\delta$. The real challenge is to prove this when $\delta=n^{-c}$ for some $c>0$. Duke, Erdős, and Rödl [DER84] proved the first statement with a $\delta^5$ in place of a $\delta^3$.
Fox and Sudakov [FoSu08b] have proved the second statement when $\delta >n^{-1/5}$. 
See also the entry in the graphs problem collection.

 I have posted a preprint giving partial results at the one-third threshold and clarifying the witness-convention issue in this problem:
Eric Li, "On the Duke--Erdős--Rödl Problem at the One-Third Threshold", arXiv:2606.06522.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06522
Write $\rho=e(G)/n^2$. The positive result is that if $\rho\geq n^{-1/3}$, equivalently if $e(G)\geq n^2/k$ with $k\leq n^{1/3}$, then $G$ contains subgraphs $H_6,H_8$ such that\[
e(H_6)=\Omega(\rho^3 n^2),\qquad e(H_8)=\Omega(\rho^2 n^2),
\]where every two distinct edges of $H_6$ lie together on a cycle of length at most $6$ contained in $H_6$, and every two distinct edges of $H_8$ lie together on a cycle of length at most $8$ contained in $H_8$.
Thus the $C_{\leq 8}$ statement is proved in the polynomial range $\rho\geq n^{-1/3}$, improving the previously recorded range $\rho>n^{-1/5}$ for that part. The same argument also gives an internal $C_{\leq 6}$ core of the expected size $\Omega(\rho^3n^2)$ in this range, but this $C_{\leq6}$ result does not impose the extra adjacent-edge $C_4$ condition from the strongest formulation of the problem.
There is also an ambient strong $C_6$ companion result. If $e(G)\geq n^2/k$ with $k=o(n^{1/2})$, then $G$ contains an edge set $F$ with\[
|F|=\Omega(n^2/k^3)
\]such that every two distinct edges of $F$ are witnessed by a cycle of length at most $6$ in the ambient graph $G$, and adjacent pairs are witnessed by ambient $C_4$'s. Here the witness cycles are allowed to use edges outside $F$.
The preprint also gives a negative result showing that the adjacent-edge $C_4$ condition is genuinely convention-sensitive. Under the internal strong $C_6$ convention, where the witnessing cycles must lie inside the subgraph and adjacent pairs must lie on $C_4$'s inside the subgraph, the bound $\Omega(\rho^3n^2)$ cannot hold at fixed polynomial densities $\rho=\Theta(n^{-\beta})$ for $\beta\in[1/3,1/2)$. More precisely, for every fixed $\beta\in[1/3,1/2)$ there are bipartite graphs $G$ with\[
e(G)=\Theta_\beta(n^{2-\beta}),\qquad \rho(G)=\Theta_\beta(n^{-\beta}),
\]such that every internally strongly $C_6$-connected subgraph $H\subseteq G$ has only\[
e(H)=O_\beta\left(\frac{\rho(G)^3n^2}{(\log n)^2}\right)
\]edges.
So the upshot is:
1. the $C_{\leq8}$ statement is proved up to the one-third threshold $\rho\geq n^{-1/3}$;
2. an internal $C_{\leq6}$ core of the expected size is also proved up to this threshold, but without the adjacent-edge $C_4$ requirement;
3. the internal strong $C_6$ version with adjacent-edge $C_4$ witnesses has a random-lift obstruction starting at the same one-third threshold.
